parsed.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 001 - The Resurrection Connection to Christian Theology - Gary Habermas with @Real Seekers

stories.title_or_label: Gary's wife's cancer diagnosis and the suffering chapter
stories.setting_or_context: Personal update at the start of the interview; Gary's wife has stage three pancreatic cancer that has progressed.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Dale asks about Gary's wife; Gary reports the diagnosis, appreciates prayers, and notes that volume 4 contains a chapter on suffering that reviewers had praised before the diagnosis.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: High pathos; personal suffering and pastoral concern.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Gary's personal circumstances and the pastoral relevance of the suffering chapter.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not provide evidence for the resurrection or for any theological claim.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Medical records contradicting the diagnosis or timeline.

stories.notes: Personal testimony used to motivate interest in the book's practical chapters.

stories.title_or_label: The skeptical softball objection: Volume 4 as presuppositionalism/appeal to emotion
stories.setting_or_context: Interview framing device: Dale presents a skeptical objection to volume 4.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Skeptics claim Gary has abandoned evidence for presuppositionalism and emotion; Gary rebuts by distinguishing the book's two halves and reaffirming evidentialism.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The rhetorical shape of the objection and Gary's denial of it.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not prove that no critic holds the objection or that Gary's self-description is accurate.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Gary's volume 4 actually relies on presuppositional or purely emotional argument.

stories.notes: Structurally load-bearing as the opening objection-response frame.

stories.title_or_label: The skeptical PhD philosopher who moved toward theism
stories.setting_or_context: Gary describes a long correspondence with a philosopher who began as an agnostic and moved toward theism while remaining agnostic about supernatural activity.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Gary answers the philosopher's questions without pushing; the philosopher moves from middle-of-the-road agnosticism to theism.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That one person reportedly moved toward theism through conversation and reading.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that evidential arguments generally produce this result or that the resurrection is true.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: The philosopher denying the account or the movement.

stories.notes: Anecdotal illustration of Gary's evidential approach.

stories.title_or_label: Russell's 'Why I Am Not a Christian' as a starting point for God and afterlife
stories.setting_or_context: Gary explains why he included a chapter on general theism and the afterlife, citing Russell's book.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Russell's book says theism requires God and an afterlife; Gary uses that as a jumping-off point for his own chapter.

boundaries.what_it_shows: Russell's stated view that theism involves God and an afterlife.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not show that Russell's view is correct or that Gary's arguments succeed.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Textual evidence that Russell did not say this.

stories.notes: Historical anecdote used to motivate the chapter structure.

stories.title_or_label: The paralytic through the roof: Jesus forgives sins and heals
stories.setting_or_context: Mark 2: a paralyzed man is lowered through a roof; Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Jesus says 'Your sins are forgiven'; scribes object that only God can forgive sins; Jesus heals the man to show he has authority on earth to forgive sins.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The narrative logic by which Jesus' healing is presented as a sign of divine authority.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not independently establish the historicity of the event or that Jesus is divine.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Historical-critical evidence that the passage is a later invention or that Jesus did not make such a claim.

stories.notes: Used as a key example of Jesus claiming deity through actions.

stories.title_or_label: Mark 14 trial: Jesus as cloud rider and seated at God's right hand
stories.setting_or_context: Mark 14:61-64: Jesus is questioned by the high priest and responds with claims that lead to a blasphemy charge.
stories.plot_or_sequence: High priest asks if Jesus is the Son of the Blessed One; Jesus says 'I am' and predicts the Son of Man coming with the clouds and seated at God's right hand; high priest tears his garments and charges blasphemy.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The narrative's presentation of Jesus making a divine claim that his opponents understood as blasphemy.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not prove the historicity of the trial scene or that Jesus actually said these words.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the passage is a later Christian invention or that the high priest's reaction is unhistorical.

stories.notes: Gary calls this the best text for Jesus claiming deity.

stories.title_or_label: The good Samaritan as radical commitment
stories.setting_or_context: Luke 10: Jesus tells the parable of the good Samaritan in response to a question about eternal life.
stories.plot_or_sequence: A man is robbed and left for dead; a Samaritan helps him, pays for his care, and Jesus says 'Go and do likewise.'

boundaries.what_it_shows: The ethical demand to love others sacrificially.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not establish the resurrection or the truth of Christianity.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the parable is not authentic to Jesus or that its ethical teaching is not binding.

stories.notes: Used to illustrate the 'radical commitment' chapter.

stories.title_or_label: The skeptic's 'future unknown natural anomaly' comeback
stories.setting_or_context: Dale presents a hypothetical: a decapitated head is restored after prayer, but skeptics say it is a natural anomaly to be explained later.
stories.plot_or_sequence: The skeptic grants the event but refuses to call it a miracle, appealing to future science; Gary responds that this move undermines empiricism and can be used against anything.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The logical problem with indefinitely deferring explanation to future science.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not prove that any particular miracle occurred or that naturalism is false.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: A demonstration that the future-unknown reply is epistemically legitimate in this case.

stories.notes: Thought experiment used to illustrate the self-undermining nature of naturalism.

stories.title_or_label: Medjugorje and the relative who never saw a miracle
stories.setting_or_context: Discussion of competing miracle claims, specifically Marian apparitions at Medjugorje.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Gary notes that despite many trips to Medjugorje, a committed believer's relative reportedly never witnessed a supernatural event; people see signs in the heavens, not Mary.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Low; anecdotal skepticism about rival claims.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That at least one person's experience at Medjugorje did not include a clear miracle.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not disprove all Marian apparitions or establish the resurrection.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the relative did witness a miracle or that the account is inaccurate.

stories.notes: Used to cast doubt on competing miracle claims.

stories.title_or_label: The Russian Orthodox friend: 'It's not the name over your door'
stories.setting_or_context: Gary recounts a conversation with a Russian Orthodox philosopher about denominational boundaries.
stories.plot_or_sequence: The friend says the Orthodox do not say 'follow us to heaven' but ask what one does with Christ, not what name is over the door.

boundaries.what_it_shows: A perspective that prioritizes Christ over denominational labels.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not settle theological disputes about which church is true.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the friend did not say this or that the Orthodox position is different.

stories.notes: Anecdote used to soften denominational divisions.

stories.title_or_label: Houdini and predicting a miracle ahead of time
stories.setting_or_context: Gary discusses the evidential value of Jesus predicting his resurrection.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Houdini was famous for announcing his escapes ahead of time, but that does not make them miracles; Jesus predicted his resurrection, which deepens the evidential force.

boundaries.what_it_shows: The difference between a predictable stunt and a one-time miracle.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: It does not prove that Jesus predicted his resurrection or that it occurred.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Houdini did not announce his escapes or that Jesus did not predict his resurrection.

stories.notes: Analogy used to highlight the uniqueness of a predicted resurrection.

narrative_arc.opening_device: Personal update about Gary's wife's cancer and the release of volume 4.
narrative_arc.central_tension: Skeptics claim volume 4 abandons evidential apologetics for presuppositionalism and emotion; Gary defends the evidential foundation and explains the theological entailments of the resurrection.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: Gary outlines the first half of volume 4, showing how the resurrection entails God, the deity of Christ, miracles, scripture, and radical commitment, while reaffirming his evidentialist method.

parsed.notes: The transcript is a conversational interview with multiple speakers. Stories are mostly illustrative or motivational; none serve as independent evidence for the resurrection. The narrative arc is driven by the objection-response structure.
